messages.subject: Avoiding memory bloat when rebuilding ggvis charts
messages.subject_clean: Avoiding memory bloat when rebuilding ggvis charts
messages.body_plain:
Hi -

[Disclaimer: I'm running on a version of ggvis that's based on the Github code as of August.  If this issue has been addressed since then, of course I'm happy to start by pulling myself up to date.]

My experiments with ggvis have now reached a stage where I want to keep my examples running for more than a few mouse clicks.  I've therefore run into the issue that every time I replace a reactive ggvis chart the memory size of my R session increases.

The effect can be seen on even a simple example such as the following demo in interactive.R (yes, the ggvis version I have predates the new props syntax):

ggvis(mtcars, props(x ~ wt, y ~ mpg),
  mark_symbol(),
  branch_smooth(
    n = input_select(
    choices = c("Two", "Six", "Eighty"),
    map = function(value) switch(value, Two = 2, Six = 6, Eighty = 80),
    label = "Number of points"
    ) ) )

If I start this from RStudio at a time when the rsession shows around 71MB in the Mac OS Activity Monitor, after the first chart has been rendered the memory size is 87MB.  After switching the Npoints drop-down ten times it's up to 90MB, and after another ten it's 101MB.  Apparently just from rebuilding the chart.

The example I'm building is considerably more complex (a reactive graph of about 20 nodes that builds two charts, one with four datasets - though all based on the tiny mtcars), and the figures correspondingly more alarming:
  initial build: 109MB
  after 10 rebuilds: 182MB
  after 20 rebuilds: 230MB

In addition to the memory bloat, the response time rises markedly: from about 0.5s for the first rebuild to over 2.0s for the 20th.

I'm still working to pin down exactly what makes up this bloat, but my assumption is that it's due to lingering reactives and observers from previous chart builds.  My code replicates the measures taken in observe_data for ensuring that old observers are suspended, and also includes tentative extensions (to Shiny) so the ggvis code can null out the dependants and functions of Observables and Observers that aren't going to be used any more... but the memory bloat remains, apparently just as bad as ever.  And the degraded response time.

Even if I eventually figure out what's preventing garbage collection of the larger objects, this kind of piecemeal nulling out of bits of the reactive structure is never going to be a long-term solution.  I guess we need a way to remove unneeded reactives and observers from the dependency structure altogether.

Does anyone have experience with doing this?  Or building mechanisms to support it?

All the best -

Aran Lunzer
Viewpoints Research

There have been a lot of changes to httpuv, shiny and ggvis since

tried your code with the latest and didn't see those problems.

Also the memory reported by the OS is a bit unreliable (as described

this function:

mem <- function() {
  bit <- 8L * .Machine$sizeof.pointer
  if (bit != 32L && bit != 64L) {
    stop("Unknown architecture", call. = FALSE)
  }

  node_size <- if (bit == 32L) 28L else 56L

  usage <- gc()
  sum(usage[, 1] * c(node_size, 8)) / (1024 ^ 2)
}
mem()

Hadley

One possible source of slowness is that the console in RStudio can get slower and slower as more text goes into the scrollback buffer. It can be cleared out with Ctrl-L. I believe that this will be remedied in the not-to-distant future. I don't think that there's anything in ggvis which should cause it to slow down as you run more plots (unless of course you use so much memory that it goes to swap).

In addition to the stuff Hadley said about memory reporting in R, there's an outstanding issue where old reactives/observers aren't always cleared out. See https://github.com/rstudio/ggvis/issues/54

A temporary workaround to clear out old reactives/observers is to run the following at the prompt (it may need to be run multiple times):
  shiny:::flushReact()

If you do this, you may also have to trigger garbage collection in order to see memory usage change:
  gc(verbose = TRUE)

I hope this helps!
-Winston

Hi - thanks for the thoughts -

In fact although we're using RStudio for code management, at runtime everything is loaded and controlled through Javascript running on a web page.

For a single set of charts a long-running Shiny app is established, exchanging messages with the JS side both through the standard web socket that connects ggvis/Shiny with Vega/JS and through a node.js-driven R command interface that uses a customised parallel.R/evaluate.R combination to pass results, warnings and errors from the running R (ggvis) code to the browser.  The memory buildup and response sluggishness is happening in this forked R session.

Perhaps it's even conceivable that something about the forked nature of the R session is interfering with the memory management?  I'm still way too new to R to tell whether that's plausible.  In any case, the R session behaves fine (no memory bloat) for operations that don't involve creating/discarding reactives - such as rapid repeated re-sending of updated Vega chart datasets.

Thank you for the pointer to the app-closing issue.  To be honest, figuring out how to close the whole application cleanly is pretty low on our priority list - especially since it's running on a forked thread, so we can just kill the thread.

I hadn't thought of using flushReact as a way to persuade reactives to drop their connections to other reactives that aren't responding any more (because we've removed their working parts).  It certainly seems like it should work, but in the current version of the code if anything it appears to have exacerbated the problem.  Perhaps that result in itself is a useful clue as to what's going on.

But for now I'm going to take a code snapshot, then wade into the upgrade/merge.  It could take some time.

Bye for now

Aran

messages.subject: Use of dscale() domain
messages.body_plain:
I'd like to create a chart axis that always starts at zero (not just includes zero), but whose domainMax is determined by the data currently being plotted.

Looking at the help for dscale and scale_quantitative, it seemed this might be achievable by specifying domain=c(0,NA).

But that didn't quite work.  The first reason was a small typo in scale.R, where the line
    named_list(paste0(name, "Min"), x[2])
should presumably read
    named_list(paste0(name, "Min"), x[1])

The second reason appears to be that Vega isn't equipped to handle a spec that has a domainMin but no domain.  The implicit domainMax is replaced by zero.

Is there in fact a way to achieve this?

The reason I don't want to do the work on the R side - figuring out the domain based on the data, such as
  domain=c(0, max(data[[xProp]]))
is that I want to be able to throw different datasets at a chart that's already up and running, and have it rescale automatically.  But still always have a zero origin.

In the absence of a kosher approach, no doubt I could stick my pointers deep into the live Vega spec and overwrite the x scale definition.  For the proof-of-concept stuff I'm building now I don't consider myself above such tactics  ;-)

Aran

ggvis(mtcars, props(x = ~wt, y = ~mpg),

  dscale("x", "numeric", domain = c(0, NA))
